title: Incorporated the Standard Oil Company with $1 million in capital
statement: In 1870 Rockefeller organized the Standard Oil Company with his brother William, Samuel Andrews, Henry M. Flagler, and Stephen V. Harkness, capitalized at $1 million, choosing the name 'Standard' to signal uniform quality in a fragmented kerosene industry.
outcome: Within two years Standard Oil controlled nearly every Cleveland refiner and two New York refineries, refining about 29,000 barrels of crude oil a day and operating its own cooperage, warehouses, and paint and glue plants.

title: Consolidated Cleveland refiners in the Cleveland Massacre
statement: Between February and March 1872, while the South Improvement Company collapsed in public controversy, Rockefeller acquired 22 of Cleveland's 26 competing refiners in less than six weeks using cash offers, stock swaps, and explicit bankruptcy threats.
outcome: Cleveland refining consolidated under Standard Oil, providing the foundation for the industrial empire Rockefeller then extended to Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and New York over the following years.

title: Created the Standard Oil Trust as a corporation of corporations
statement: On January 2, 1882, 41 investors signed the Standard Oil Trust Agreement, pooling securities of 40 separately incorporated companies into a single holding vehicle managed by nine trustees, with an initial valuation of $70 million; the legal architecture is widely credited to Standard Oil's general solicitor Samuel Calvin Tate Dodd.
outcome: The trust structure let Rockefeller centralize control across state lines despite Ohio's restrictive corporation law; rival businesses rapidly copied the device, seeding the great trust wave of Gilded Age American industry and the antitrust reaction that ultimately undid it.

title: Dissolved by the U.S. Supreme Court under the Sherman Antitrust Act
statement: On May 15, 1911, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously upheld a lower court decree ordering Standard Oil of New Jersey broken into 34 separate companies, with Chief Justice White's majority opinion introducing the 'rule of reason' standard for evaluating industrial combinations under the Sherman Act.
outcome: The severed entities, with a combined net value of roughly $375 million, became the ancestors of ExxonMobil, Chevron, BP, and other major oil companies; paradoxically, Rockefeller's personal wealth multiplied after the breakup as the spinoffs gained value as separately traded equities.

title: Chartered the Rockefeller Foundation to promote global well-being
statement: In 1913 Rockefeller established the Rockefeller Foundation, chartered in New York to 'promote the well-being of mankind throughout the world,' as the capstone of a sequence of philanthropic institutions he had been building since 1901, including the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, the General Education Board, and the Rockefeller Sanitary Commission.
outcome: The Foundation's International Health Division worked in 52 countries on hookworm, malaria, and yellow fever; built and endowed the first school of hygiene and public health at Johns Hopkins; spent roughly $25 million seeding public-health schools globally; and catalyzed the Mexico agricultural program that became the Green Revolution.
